svg.aria-label: Diagram: A CloudWatch Synthetics canary is a configurable script that runs on a schedule, and it answers a question a metric alarm cannot, because canaries follow the same routes and perform the same actions as a customer, making it possible to verify customer experience even when there is no customer traffic. The trade is where the signal comes from. A metric alarm's signal is produced by the thing being watched, so it keeps arriving while the watcher is fine. A canary's signal is produced by the watcher, so it stops when either the service or the canary breaks, and the alarm reports INSUFFICIENT_DATA in both cases. Canary metrics are published per run in the CloudWatchSynthetics namespace with CanaryName as a dimension, so a canary that is stopped, paused, or broken by its own script update emits no new datapoints. Following that into the alarm rules: the evaluation range fills with missing data, the default treatment is missing, an all-missing range transitions the alarm to INSUFFICIENT_DATA, and because an alarm invokes actions only when it changes state, the ALARM action never fires. INSUFFICIENT_DATA is a state CloudWatch distinguishes from OK, but a notification wired only to ALARM does not deliver it, which is why a canary alarm should set missing-data treatment to breaching, where missing points are treated as bad and breaching the threshold. Three metrics read like synonyms and are not. Failed counts canary runs that failed to execute and those failures are related to the canary itself, so it is a statement about your monitoring. SuccessPercent is the percentage of runs that succeed and find no failures, describing the first attempt against the service. SuccessPercentWithRetries is the percentage that succeed after all attempts, with RetryCount displayed only when retries occur, so a path that fails then succeeds on retry scores badly on one and perfectly on the other. Failed requests counts HTTP requests that failed with no response rather than runs, so a 500 response is not a failed request by that definition. Available dimensions depend on the canary's own configuration: browser-dimension metrics are enabled by default for multi-browser canaries and disabled by default for single-browser ones, and step dimensions exist only for canaries using executeStep or executeHttpStep, so alarms on Browser or StepName are coupled to the script with nothing linking them. Canaries can run as often as once per minute, which is 1,440 Lambda invocations a day. The conclusion is an availability alarm treating missing data as breaching plus a separate alarm on Failed, and because Failed also stops publishing when the canary is not running at all, canary scheduling and execution status has to be monitored separately.
svg.title: A canary's signal stops when either the service or the canary breaks
svg.text: The signal is produced by the watcher. So its silence has two causes.
“Canaries follow the same routes and perform the same actions as a customer … even when you don’t have any
customer traffic on your applications.”
METRIC ALARM ON REAL TRAFFIC
Signal comes from the watched thing.
Keeps arriving while the watcher is fine.
But cannot tell working from unused.
CANARY
Signal comes from the watcher.
Stops when EITHER one breaks.
Both cases land in INSUFFICIENT_DATA.
The chain, from #110
canary stops → no runs → no datapoints → evaluation range all missing
→ default treatment is “missing” → INSUFFICIENT_DATA
→ “actions only when the alarm changes state” → nothing fires
Fix: set the canary alarm to breaching. Absence means visibility is lost — which is itself worth paging on.
Three metrics that read like synonyms
Failed runs that “failed to execute … related to the canary itself”
SuccessPercent runs that “succeed and find no failures” — first attempt
SuccessPercentWithRetries runs that “succeed after all attempts” — path usable?
Failed is about your monitoring. The other two are about your service, and they disagree on purpose.
And the dimensions depend on the canary’s own configuration
Browser metrics default ON for multi-browser canaries, OFF for single-browser. StepName exists only with
executeStep() or executeHttpStep(). A script refactor can silently remove the metric an alarm watches.
Two alarms, plus the schedule itself.
One on availability, treating missing data as breaching. One on Failed. Missing datapoints mean visibility is lost,
not that the application is unwell. Failed stops publishing too, so monitor scheduling and execution status.
Once per minute is 1,440 Lambda invocations a day. Set the schedule from how long you can afford not to know.
